paragraph: The S&P 500 -- the index that tracks 500 large U.S. companies -- closed at 7,720, about 5.7% above its long-term trend line. Above that line is what people mean by a bull market: prices rising over months, not just days. Today's news flow leans cautious -- more focused on avoiding losses than on chasing gains. The loudest themes in the headlines: Middle East Tension, Trump Tariff Negative, Health Outbreak. Put trend and headlines together and the combined read is 'risk-on': conditions favour patience with a plan over reacting to any single headline.
what_it_means: A bull trend describes the recent past. It is not a forecast, and it has never once meant 'prices only go up from here.'
When the news turns defensive, prices often move on fear and relief instead of on how businesses are actually doing. That kind of noise is normal -- it is most of what daily market news is.
Earnings season is when companies publish their real numbers -- sales, profit, debt. It is the regular reality check behind the stories told about stocks the rest of the time.
Trouble in oil-producing regions moves energy prices first, and everything that runs on fuel after that -- one reason it leads market news even if you never think about oil.
This digest is market vocabulary in plain English, for learning only -- never a tip on what to buy or sell.
